lessons.title: The Vietnam War 1965-1973
lessons.description: Search and destroy, Tet, My Lai, Vietnamisation — US and Vietcong tactics and the war's collapse.
lessons.content_html:
US Military Strategy: Search and Destroy

General William Westmoreland commanded US forces and adopted a “search and destroy” strategy, using superior firepower and mobility to kill enemy fighters rather than hold territory. US forces used helicopters to insert troops into enemy areas, then withdrew, measuring progress through body counts. The strategy reflected a belief that the USA’s technological advantage would ultimately overwhelm the Vietcong.

The USA also deployed Agent Orange, a chemical defoliant, to strip jungle cover from Vietcong supply routes, and dropped napalm on villages suspected of sheltering enemy fighters. Free-fire zones were designated areas where US troops could shoot at anyone, on the assumption that all residents were hostile. These tactics caused significant civilian casualties.

Key Fact

Operation Rolling Thunder (1965–1968) dropped more bombs on Vietnam than US forces had dropped in the entire Pacific theatre of the Second World War. Despite this firepower, the Vietcong continued to recruit and resupply through the Ho Chi Minh Trail, demonstrating the limits of aerial bombardment against a guerrilla enemy.

Vietcong Tactics

North Vietnamese General Vo Nguyen Giap and the Vietcong relied on guerrilla tactics: ambushes, booby traps, hit-and-run raids and a network of underground tunnels at Cu Chi near Saigon. Vietcong fighters were indistinguishable from civilians, making the identification of the enemy extremely difficult for US forces.

The Vietcong also used political terror against village headmen loyal to the South Vietnamese government, and drew on a deep well of nationalist sentiment that resented both the Saigon government and the presence of foreign troops. Giap understood that the USA could not sustain indefinite casualties politically, even if it could militarily: the strategy was to make the war too costly for America to continue.

On 31 January 1968, at the start of the Vietnamese lunar new year (Tet), North Vietnamese and Vietcong forces launched coordinated surprise attacks on more than 100 South Vietnamese towns and cities, including Saigon. The Tet Offensive was militarily repulsed; the attackers suffered massive casualties. But it shattered American public confidence. General Westmoreland had been assuring the public the war was being won; the Tet Offensive proved the enemy was far from defeated. President Johnson’s approval rating collapsed and on 31 March 1968 he announced he would not seek re-election.

On 16 March 1968, US soldiers killed hundreds of unarmed civilians — including women, children and elderly people — in the village of My Lai. The My Lai massacre was covered up initially and not reported publicly until November 1969. When it became known, it intensified domestic and international opposition to the war. It raised fundamental moral questions about the conduct of US forces and the effect of free-fire zone policies on military behaviour.

Vietnamisation and Withdrawal

President Richard Nixon took office in January 1969 and introduced the Vietnamisation policy: gradually withdrawing US troops while training South Vietnamese forces to take over the fighting. US troop numbers fell from 543,000 in 1969 to under 50,000 by 1972. At the same time Nixon secretly bombed and then invaded Cambodia to destroy supply routes.

In May 1970, National Guard troops shot four students dead at Kent State University during an anti-war protest. The killings provoked mass demonstrations across American campuses. In 1971, Daniel Ellsberg leaked the Pentagon Papers to the press, revealing that successive administrations had deliberately misled Congress and the public about the war’s conduct and origins.

Key Fact

The Paris Peace Accords were signed in January 1973, and the last US combat troops left Vietnam in March 1973. US forces had not been defeated on the battlefield, but domestic political pressure, the Tet Offensive’s psychological impact, and the credibility damage of My Lai and the Pentagon Papers made continued involvement untenable.

Opposition to the Vietnam War built steadily from the mid-1960s. College campuses became centres of anti-war activity; draft card burning and sit-ins spread across the country. Television coverage brought the war’s violence directly into American homes in a way no previous conflict had allowed. When Eddie Adams’s photograph of the execution of a Vietcong prisoner on the streets of Saigon was published in February 1968, it became an iconic image of the war’s moral complexity.

The anti-war movement was diverse: it included students, civil rights activists (Martin Luther King Jr. opposed the war from 1967, arguing it diverted resources from domestic poverty), veterans who had served in Vietnam, and mainstream Democrats disillusioned with Johnson’s credibility gap. The movement did not end the war directly, but it constrained the options available to Nixon, who knew that any significant re-escalation would trigger massive domestic unrest. It demonstrated that in a democratic society, public opinion ultimately sets the boundaries of military action.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about Vietnam tactics, examiners want both US and Vietcong tactics treated factually and without characterising either side as the ‘aggressor’. Describe Agent Orange, napalm and free-fire zones alongside Vietcong tunnel systems and political terror — the examiner is looking for balance and specific evidence. For questions about US withdrawal, link the military tactics (Vietnamisation) to the domestic political pressure (Tet, My Lai, Kent State, Pentagon Papers) — neither explanation works on its own without the other.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • US tactics — search and destroy, Agent Orange, napalm, free-fire zones — caused significant civilian casualties and failed to defeat a guerrilla enemy who relied on tunnels, ambushes and political support from the population.
  • The Tet Offensive (January 1968) and the My Lai massacre (March 1968, reported 1969) destroyed public confidence in the war effort and contributed directly to LBJ’s decision not to seek re-election.
  • Nixon’s Vietnamisation gradually withdrew US combat troops; the last left in March 1973 following the Paris Peace Accords, but domestic opposition — accelerated by Kent State and the Pentagon Papers — had made continued involvement politically impossible.

lessons.title: End of the war and its international legacy
lessons.description: Fall of Saigon, détente and how Cold War historians have debated who was responsible.
lessons.content_html:
The Fall of Saigon 1975

Following the withdrawal of US combat troops in March 1973, the Paris Peace Accords left South Vietnam to defend itself against a continuing North Vietnamese military campaign. The South Vietnamese government received continued US financial support but no military intervention. In early 1975, North Vietnamese forces launched a major offensive. On 30 April 1975, Saigon fell. Dramatic footage of US helicopters evacuating the last Americans from the roof of the embassy transmitted a powerful image of defeat around the world. Vietnam was reunified under communist rule as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam.

The legacy of the war for the USA was profound. Approximately 58,000 American soldiers had died; South Vietnam had lost far more. The conflict exposed the limits of American military power, damaged public trust in government, and produced a generation of veterans dealing with physical and psychological injuries. Congress passed the War Powers Act in 1973, requiring the President to notify Congress within 48 hours of deploying forces and limiting deployments to 60 days without congressional approval.

Key Fact

Saigon fell on 30 April 1975. The USA had lost approximately 58,000 soldiers in a war that ended in the victory of the side it had fought against. The War Powers Act (1973) was Congress’s direct response to the way the President had bypassed congressional approval throughout the conflict.

Détente and the Relaxation of Tensions 1969–1979

Alongside the Vietnam War, a broader shift in superpower relations was underway. Détente — the French word for “relaxation” — described a policy of managing rather than winning the Cold War through negotiation. Nixon and his National Security Adviser Henry Kissinger led this approach. In February 1972 Nixon made a landmark visit to communist China, opening diplomatic relations after more than two decades of hostility. This triangular diplomacy played the USSR against China, exploiting the Sino-Soviet split.

In May 1972, Nixon and Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev signed the SALT I agreement, the first treaty to limit the growth of nuclear weapons. It froze the number of intercontinental ballistic missiles and submarine-launched ballistic missiles. The Helsinki Accords of 1975, signed by 35 nations, recognised the existing European borders established after 1945 and included a commitment to human rights that Soviet dissidents later used to challenge the Kremlin.

Détente ended abruptly in December 1979 when the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan to prop up a communist government. The USA boycotted the 1980 Moscow Olympics and Carter withdrew the SALT II treaty from Senate ratification. The invasion marked the return of intense superpower competition, sometimes called the “Second Cold War”. The episode showed how the structure of détente — based on negotiation rather than shared values — was vulnerable to a single decisive military action.

Cold War Historiography: Orthodox, Revisionist and Post-Revisionist

Historians have debated responsibility for the Cold War across three broad schools of thought. The orthodox school, dominant in the 1950s and 1960s, blamed Soviet expansionism: Stalin’s takeover of Eastern Europe and his hostile ideology made the Cold War inevitable. Early Cold War historians such as Arthur Schlesinger Jr. held this view.

From the 1960s, revisionist historians such as William Appleman Williams shifted emphasis toward American responsibility, arguing that US economic expansionism — the “Open Door” policy — and atomic diplomacy provoked Soviet defensiveness rather than Soviet aggression causing the conflict. The Vietnam War and revelations about CIA activities deepened public receptiveness to this reading.

Key Fact

The post-revisionist school, developed by John Lewis Gaddis from the 1970s, rejected simple blame narratives. Gaddis argued that both superpowers pursued their own interests and that the Cold War arose from their interaction, not from one side’s aggression alone. Post-Cold War access to Soviet archives from the 1990s gave historians new evidence that largely supported post-revisionist conclusions.

The interpretation of appeasement has also shifted across three schools. The Guilty Men reading, originating in Michael Foot’s 1940 pamphlet, condemned Chamberlain and other appeasers as culpably naive men who handed Hitler advantage after advantage. A.J.P. Taylor’s revisionist approach in “The Origins of the Second World War” (1961) argued that appeasement reflected the genuine popular desire to avoid another catastrophic war — the “Popular Majority” view. More recent revisionist work by R.A.C. Parker argued that Chamberlain had genuine strategic alternatives that he refused to explore, making appeasement a deliberate choice rather than an inevitable response to public pressure.

Examiners reward students who can name these schools and anchor each to specific evidence: for Guilty Men, the Munich Agreement and Chamberlain’s claim of “peace for our time”; for the Popular Majority reading, public opinion polls of 1938; for the Parker revisionist reading, the rejected Soviet alliance proposals of 1939. Quoting a phrase from a given interpretation and linking it to one of these schools is the key technique for the highest band.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When evaluating a historical interpretation, the top band requires you to quote a phrase from the extract and link it explicitly to a named school (e.g. “this reflects the orthodox school because...”). Examiners specifically reward students who can name these schools — do not write “some historians think” when you can name Gaddis or Williams.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Saigon fell on 30 April 1975, ending the Vietnam War; the defeat damaged US credibility and led to the 1973 War Powers Act limiting presidential authority to deploy forces without Congress.
  • Détente (1969–1979) brought SALT I (1972), Nixon’s opening of China, and the Helsinki Accords (1975), but ended when the USSR invaded Afghanistan in December 1979.
  • Cold War historiography has three main schools: orthodox (Soviet blame, 1950s), revisionist (US blame, Williams 1960s), and post-revisionist (mutual interaction, Gaddis 1970s onwards) — post-Cold War Soviet archives broadly supported the post-revisionist reading.
